newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - High yielders in EMU firing line again.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - High yielders in EMU firing line again.

text.p: European single currency woes and the French election will lash high yielding debt markets this week but how long the sting will last was unclear, analysts said on Tuesday.

Some analysts saw any spread widening resulting from crucial European Commission deficit forecasts on Wednesday as a chance to shop. Others said debt yields of markets like Italy and Spain have come as close as they are going to get to German yields this year.

"I would use the weakness as an opportunity to buy," said Paul Meader, managing director at Rothschild Bank Switzerland C.I. in Guernsey. "I don't think we're going to see the start of a big new trend."

The European Commission was set to release 1997/98 economic and budget forecasts -- including key deficit-to-GDP and debt-to-GDP estimates -- on Wednesday. A deficit should be no more than three percent of GDP and debt no more than 60 percent to qualify for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

Market talk has grown that the core EMU countries like Germany will not meet the targets, let alone the high yielders after a Portuguese newspaper report on April 10. The paper reported that the EC would forecast Germany's 1997 budget deficit at 3.2 percent and Italy's at 3.8 percent.

Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer intensified speculation about the forecasts when he said late on Monday a delay to EMU could be considered if it became clear big countries would fail to meet the convergence criteria.
"The actual forecasts that come out are going to be very important certainly after we heard Tietmeyer's comments last night," Brian Venables, bond strategist at ABN-AMRO in Amsterdam, said.
Analysts said the French election, now confirmed for May 25 and June 1, will also cast a pall over the whole EMU process and delay further convergence by high yielders.
"We expect whoever wins it to be pro-EMU, but if the Socialists win they will be less accomodating to the Germans and more accomodating to Spain and Italy," Venables said.

Both Meader and Venables, however, did not expect the spreads of Italy, Spain, Sweden and Portugal against Bunds to push out much further from where they were currently at 180 basis points, 110, 145, and 97 respectively.
Venables saw Italy hitting around 190 basis points and Meader said 200 would likely cap the widening. The prospect of Italian interest rate cuts would mediate EMU woes, they added.

Meader said the political drive for EMU has formed the rationale for his strategy and would continue to do so. He targets 50 basis points on the BTP/Bund spread by the end of the year, admitting he was more bullish than most.
"At the end of the day, the decisions that will be taken about EMU will be political, not economic. I expect the first round of EMU to happen on time with a broad range of countries," he said.
He added by 1999, economic cycles would favour the high yielders which would still be needing interest rate cuts while German rates would be on the way up.
Kirit Shah, chief market strategist at Sanwa International in London, did not think the spreads would spring back so quickly.

"My preferred strategy is to sell into strength rather than to buy into weakness," he said. "The medium risk factors have been enlarged. One is the French election uncertainly, second the dollar, and third the general concerns over EMU, especially for Spain and Italy," he said.

"Although inflation is very positive and yes they have been able to cut rates, the big picture is still very uncertain in terms of the EMU risk factors. I'm not enthusiastic for further convergence in the near term. We are unlikely to see the highs of this year (in price terms) for Spain and Italy," he said.
